Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a practical “recipe” you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your CI/CD pipeline).  
I’ll walk through each numbered step, show the exact shell commands, and give you ready‑to‑copy templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow.  

> **⚠️ Important** – I don’t have access to your machine or the network, so I can’t actually run `git clone` or `git push`.  
> The commands below assume you’re working on a Unix‑like shell (Linux/macOS) or PowerShell on Windows.  
> If you’re on Windows and prefer PowerShell, replace `bash` syntax with PowerShell equivalents (`git clone`, `git add`, etc.).

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1.1 Create a working directory (optional)
mkdir ~/projects && cd ~/projects

# 1.2 Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> *If you’re cloning over HTTPS instead of SSH, use:*  
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Detect the predominant language

> **Why** – Knowing the language lets us pick the right base image and runtime flags.  
> **How** – Run a quick scan with `linguist` (GitHub’s language detection tool) or a simple `find` + `wc` script.

```bash
# Install linguist if you don’t already have it
gem install github-linguist

# Scan the repo (excluding README, docs, tests, etc.)
linguist --json . > linguist_report.json

# Inspect the JSON to see the dominant language
cat linguist_report.json | jq '.languages'
```

> *If you don’t want to install Ruby gems, you can use the `detect-language` npm package or a custom script.*

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

> **Assumption** – The repo is a Node.js app (based on the repo name).  
> If the analysis shows a different language, adjust the base image accordingly.

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile (nodejs-welcome/Dockerfile)

# 2.2.1 Pick a lightweight base image
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# 2.2.2 Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# 2.2.3 Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# 2.2.4 Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# 2.2.5 Copy source code
COPY . .

# 2.2.6 Build the app (if needed)
RUN npm run build || true

# 2.2.7 Final stage (multi‑stage build)
FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app /app

# 2.2.8 Expose the port the app listens on (adjust if your app uses a different port)
EXPOSE 3000

# 2.2.9 Default command
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *If the repo uses Yarn, replace `npm` with `yarn` and adjust the install/build commands.*

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a `k8s` folder to keep things tidy:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

#### Deployment (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### Service (`k8s/service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to ClusterIP or NodePort if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80           # External port
    targetPort: 3000   # Container port
```

> *If you’re deploying to a cluster that doesn’t support external load balancers (e.g., Minikube), change `type` to `NodePort` and note the assigned node port.*

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: |
          k8s/deployment.yaml
          k8s/service.yaml
        images: |
          zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}   # Base64‑encoded kubeconfig
```

> *Make sure you store the following secrets in your GitHub repo settings → Secrets → Actions:*
> - `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME`
> - `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` (a personal access token with `write:packages` scope)
> - `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` (Base64‑encoded kubeconfig for your cluster)

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
# Stage everything (including new Dockerfile, k8s folder, and workflow)
git add Dockerfile k8s/.github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> *If you only want to add specific files, list them explicitly:*
> `git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml`

---

## 4️⃣ Commit and push

```bash
# 4.1 Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4.2 Push to the remote
git push origin main
```

> *If you’re on a protected branch that requires a pull request, skip the direct push and open a PR instead:*
> ```bash
> git push origin HEAD:new-feature-branch
> gh pr create --fill   # Requires GitHub CLI
> ```

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, verify that:

1. **GitHub Actions** shows a successful run under the *Actions* tab.  
2. The Docker image appears in Docker Hub (or your chosen registry).  
3. The Kubernetes manifests apply cleanly:  
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/
   ```
4. The service is reachable (check the external IP or node port).

---

## Recap of the files you now have

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── Dockerfile
├── k8s/
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   └── service.yaml
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        └── ci.yml
```

Feel free to tweak the Dockerfile (e.g., add health checks, multi‑stage builds for static assets) or the Kubernetes manifests (add liveness/readiness probes, resource limits, autoscaling) to suit your production needs. Happy coding!
